title: Due diligence prerequisite before investing
claim: Before committing capital to a stock, the investor must conduct foundational research to understand the business and validate assumptions.
support: Author frames Rule 1 as a required prerequisite; emphasizes 'don't leave home without doing it.'
mechanism: Reduces probability of investing in fundamentally unsound companies; screens for basic viability.
assumptions: Market reward compounds with better stock selection
Public financial data is accessible and interpretable
failure_modes: Over-reliance on financial statements without forward-looking analysis
Excessive analysis paralysis delaying entry

title: Margin trading amplifies both gains and losses
claim: Using leverage via margin accounts multiplies profit and loss; losses can exceed capital if price moves unfavorably.
support: Author discusses margin account requirements and forced liquidation mechanics; emphasizes double-edged risk.
mechanism: Leverage scales P&L; margin calls force position closure if equity falls below broker requirement.
assumptions: Margin requirements remain static
Broker will not fail or restrict liquidity
failure_modes: Gap risk: market gaps through stop levels on low liquidity
Forced liquidation in stressed markets
Negative equity if gap opens beyond margin cushion

title: CFDs enable short selling more easily than direct stocks
claim: Contracts for difference (CFDs) allow short selling by default; many stock brokers restrict short selling or limit available shares.
support: Author notes CFD structure (contract vs. asset) removes friction; direct short selling faces broker restrictions or impossible borrowing.
mechanism: CFD is OTC derivative; no borrow fee negotiation required; broker controls both sides.
assumptions: CFD broker does not restrict short selling
Counterparty risk of CFD broker is acceptable
failure_modes: CFD broker insolvency
Forced position closure due to liquidity crisis
Overnight gaps in CFD pricing vs. spot

title: Buying on down days can amplify losses if downtrend continues
claim: Accumulating stock on declining days assumes reversion; if decline persists, capital is exhausted before recovery.
support: Author cautions against unbounded down-day accumulation; illustrates risk of doubling down in extended bear market.
mechanism: Pyramiding into losers consumes cash reserves; ruin risk if capital is finite and decline is severe/prolonged.
assumptions: Market will reverse to profitable level
Capital reserves are sufficient for full accumulation sequence
failure_modes: Margin call if using leverage
Emotional breakdown under repeated losses
Permanent capital loss if company fails

title: Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) exposes investors to bear market drawdown if horizon is too short
claim: Monthly fixed-amount investing does not protect against multi-year bear markets; 7-14 year horizon required to see two full economic cycles.
support: Author criticizes DCA as 'idiot-proof' marketing; warns that 1-3 years of DCA in bear market can lose 50% or more.
mechanism: DCA assumes long-term uptrend or mean-reversion; shorter horizons (<7 years) risk realizing losses in trough of cycle.
assumptions: Economic cycles exist and are ~7-14 years
Investor will not liquidate in downturn
failure_modes: Portfolio liquidated at peak drawdown
Psychological capitulation during bear market
Sequence-of-returns risk early in accumulation

title: Stop-loss placement requires alignment with trading timeframe
claim: Longer-term traders should use wider stops than day traders; stop placement reflects expected volatility and risk tolerance.
support: Author uses example: day chart setups warrant intra-day stops; swing trades warrant wider stops based on support/resistance.
mechanism: Wide stops reduce whipsaw frequency; tight stops improve risk/reward on intraday noise but increase false exit rate.
assumptions: Historical volatility is stable
Support/resistance levels are predictive of mean reversion
failure_modes: Gap risk bypasses stop on adverse news
Emotional override of predetermined stop levels

title: Risk-reward ratio should match holding period
claim: Longer-term trades warrant higher profit targets to justify larger stops; risk-reward ratio must be maintained per timeframe.
support: Author argues that tight stop + large position = high risk; loose stop + loose target maintains acceptable risk per unit.
mechanism: Risk-reward tradeoff: if stop is 2% away, target should be ≥4% to justify the bet; scales with holding period.
assumptions: Market offers sufficient opportunity to meet target
Slippage and commissions are acceptable on wider stops
failure_modes: Excessive drawdown from repeated 1:1 risk-reward trades
Missed target leads to breakeven or loss

title: Fundamental analysis is primary filter; technical analysis is precision tool for entry/exit
claim: Author uses fundamental analysis to build watchlist, then technical analysis to time entry and set stops/targets.
support: Author explicitly states: 'fundamental analysis with grunt work leads the way for my short list; technical analysis gives me pricing levels to execute.'
mechanism: Fundamental filters reduce search space from thousands to dozens; technical analysis removes timing/execution guesswork.
assumptions: Technical patterns are predictive
Fundamental screen selects quality names
Combination reduces false signals vs. either alone
failure_modes: Fundamental screen over-fits to historical criteria
Technical patterns break in regime shift
Watchlist becomes stale

title: Multi-timeframe confirmation improves trade quality but delays entry
claim: Confirming setup on higher timeframe (week/month) before entering on lower timeframe (day/hour) reduces false signals but increases entry slippage.
support: Author describes looking at daily chart for sideways movement, weekly for weak downtrend, and monthly for strong downtrend; merges signals to trade short on resistance on daily bounce.
mechanism: Higher timeframe alignment acts as regime filter; increases conviction and reduces noise, but price may move away before lower timeframe signal.
assumptions: Higher timeframe trends persist
Lower timeframe noise is decorrelated from trend
failure_modes: Missed opportunity: price trends away before lower timeframe signal
Whipsaw if higher timeframe reverses

title: Limit orders on high-timeframe confirmation trades off entry certainty for price improvement
claim: Author uses limit orders on higher-timeframe signals to avoid paying market price; accepts risk of missing trade entirely for better fill.
support: Author describes parking limit orders at support/resistance levels and willingly forgoing trade if price does not retrace to limit.
mechanism: Market order = guaranteed fill + worse price; limit order = possible no-fill + better price if filled; author chooses latter for conviction trades.
assumptions: Price will retrace to limit within reasonable time
Foregoing trade has no regret if it trends away
failure_modes: Stock zooms away; limit never hit and trade is missed
Emotional regret of watching missed run-up
Opportunity cost of capital sitting idle

title: Fibonacci ratios 0.618 and 1.618 are primary technical levels
claim: Author focuses on Fibonacci extensions (0.618, 1.618) rather than retracements (0.382, 0.236) to avoid chart clutter and improve clarity.
support: Author cites personal experience: 'I have come to realize these are the more potent and accurate numbers' vs. other Fibonacci levels.
mechanism: Fibonacci ratios reflect golden-ratio proportions observed in nature; hypothesis is price action respects these levels.
assumptions: Fibonacci levels are predictive of support/resistance
Market participants recognize and trade Fibonacci levels
failure_modes: Fibonacci levels break in trending market
Too-narrow focus misses other valid levels

title: Turning points in price chart are key to Fibonacci placement
claim: Identifying price turning points (valleys/peaks) correctly is critical for applying Fibonacci retracements; higher timeframes improve turning point spotting.
support: Author notes turning points are where price reverses from up-to-down or down-to-up; weekly/monthly charts show clearer turning points than intraday.
mechanism: Fibonacci retracement lines are drawn from turning point A to turning point B; incorrect turning points lead to misaligned levels.
assumptions: Turning points are objectively identifiable
Historical turning points predict future support/resistance
failure_modes: Subjective turning point identification leads to multiple valid readings
Turning points shift as new data arrives (right-edge bias)

title: Trading psychology and impulse control are critical to strategy execution
claim: Author emphasizes that proper trade planning (risk-first mindset) and discipline are more important than strategy optimality.
support: Author recounts early mistakes: entering based on hope/wishful thinking; now all trades start with 'how much can we lose'; facts over hope.
mechanism: Pre-trade risk definition reduces emotional override; removes hope/regret loops that lead to missed stops or over-leveraging.
assumptions: Trader can maintain discipline
Pre-defined rules will be followed
failure_modes: Inability to follow rules under stress
Regret and revenge trading after loss
Deviation from system under FOMO

title: Stock screeners reduce universe but still require manual curation
claim: Automated stock screeners help filter thousands of stocks to hundreds, but final selection still requires human judgment.
support: Author notes screeners eliminate much tedium but acknowledge 'sometimes you really got to crawl through a few hundred companies.'
mechanism: Screeners filter by objective rules (P/E, ROE, etc.); final selection requires assessing quality, moat, management.
assumptions: Screen criteria are predictive
Manual judgment adds alpha
failure_modes: Screen criteria are backward-looking
Manual curation introduces bias/errors

title: Insider and institutional trades are market signals but hard to monitor at scale
claim: Author notes that monitoring insider/institutional trades is valuable but introduces cognitive burden; prefers to rely on technical analysis of final outcome.
support: Author: 'Imagine monitoring fifty stocks and tracking insider trades...that drove me up the wall. Simpler to use technical analysis.'
mechanism: Insider/institutional buying predicts upside; but real-time data is sparse and expensive; technical analysis aggregates all information in price.
assumptions: Price action reflects insider knowledge
Insider trades are tradeable at retail scale
failure_modes: Information asymmetry: insiders have non-public data
Insider trades may be motivated by non-price factors (hedging, tax loss harvesting)

title: Trading on lower timeframes increases noise but speeds execution
claim: Five-minute chart trades fill faster but have higher false-signal rate vs. daily-chart trades.
support: Author prefers daily-chart entries over 5-min entries; notes 15 five-minute trades feels less satisfying than 1 daily trade; acknowledges different psychology.
mechanism: Intraday noise is high; frequent entries exhaust capital and attention; daily entries reduce overhead.
assumptions: Trader prefers fewer, higher-conviction trades
Lower timeframe signal quality degrades with shorter horizon
failure_modes: High-frequency trading exhausts capital on commissions
Emotional exhaustion from constant monitoring
Over-optimization of intraday patterns

title: Author advocates for quality-over-quantity in trade execution
claim: Fewer, high-confidence trades based on multiple timeframe alignment and plan discipline outperform high-frequency, low-conviction entries.
support: Author recurring theme: 'I know there will always be a next one coming...I can simply wait for the next better one.'
mechanism: Discipline to wait for aligned signals reduces tail risk and regret; fewer but better trades improve Sharpe-like metrics.
assumptions: Aligned signals are reliably more profitable
Opportunity cost of waiting is acceptable
failure_modes: Over-selectivity misses alpha opportunities
Market regime change breaks correlation between timeframes
